question: Following a previous question1 on the need to strengthen the connectivity and territorial cohesion of islands, the Commission responded that it ‘is not proposing a separate financial mechanism or measures exclusively for the connectivity of islands’. Its position fails to address the permanent and structural nature of the handicaps recognised by Article 174 TFEU.

2 Taking into account that the permanent additional costs of island living constitute a form of structural market failure and justify the adoption of specific, permanent compensatory mechanisms and fiscal instruments (such as reduced VAT and the transport equivalent) and adapted state aid rules for all islands, and that the implementation of European measures to decarbonise air and maritime transport (ReFuelEU aviation and ETS) may disproportionately burden island regions, increasing transport costs and limiting their connectivity in the absence of appropriate transitional and compensatory measures: 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose specific European compensation mechanisms to address the permanent additional costs of island living,3 in particular in the areas of transport, energy and the provision of essential public services?

Does the Commission plan to adapt the EU state aid framework, including the de minimis rule, the General Block Exemption Regulation and regional aid rules, to take sufficient account of the permanent structural handicaps and increased operating costs of island economies?
Does the Commission intend to introduce specific measures to offset the impact of decarbonisation policies for air and maritime transport on island regions?4
See E-000173/2026 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000173_EN.html.

The state of being an island creates structural problems of dependence on maritime and air transport, which constitute a public service on which the daily life of European citizens living on islands depends, with additional costs for the import and export of goods and raw materials, mainly for energy and consumer products, as well as for the transport of passengers.

3 These mechanisms should include specific financial instruments and adapted regulatory frameworks to address the additional costs related to transport, maritime and air connections, energy, market access and the provision of public services. 4 Such as, for example, protecting accessible and reliable connectivity, maintaining public service obligations and using ETS revenues to support island transport systems. 1 2
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2026) The EU’s State aid frameworks1 give Member States the possibility to provide islands with tailored support in view of the structurally higher costs they face. The proposals for the General Block Exemption Regulation2 (GBER) and the Air Transport Guidelines3 continue to support island airports.

Among the provisions under discussion in the GBER revision is an increase in the eligibility threshold for airport aid from 200 000 to 500 000 yearly passengers. Airports located on islands can also benefit from higher aid intensities for their investments.

In addition, the proposals for the GBER and the Air Transport Guidelines explicitly consider the complexity of maritime connections between islands and the mainland. The ongoing reviews of the relevant State aid frameworks provide an opportunity to assess comments, as appropriate, on the need to cater for island specificities.

Public Service Obligations4 (PSOs) facilitate maritime connections and can help offset some of the additional costs that islands face as a result of their insularity. For example, in Greece, the PSO in the electricity sector provides a subsidy mechanism that spreads the extra cost of supplying non-interconnected islands across all consumers, helping to keep island electricity prices lower.

The EU is also investing in island interconnections to reduce those costs over time and support decarbonisation. To reduce costs, the Emissions Trading System5 and FuelEU Maritime6 allow Member States to exempt voyages servicing small islands from their scope.

Finally, the EU strategy for islands7, sets out a forward-looking action for the Commission to launch an in-depth analysis of the cost of insularity and best practice measures to mitigate it, notably in the transport sector.

1 2014 Aviation Guidelines, the General Block Exemption Regulation, and the Regional Aid Guidelines. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/651/oj/eng. 3 https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/public-consultations/2026-air-transport-guidelines_en. 4 https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-modes/air/internal-market/public-service-obligations-psos_en. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/959/oj/eng.
